also: what case does this preposition take?

evidence: Quint. 1.7.5: ut ad, cum esset praepositiō, d litteram … acciperet
terms.comment: The word “put before” its noun, and also the prefix put before a verb: Quintilian’s compound words aut praepositiōnibus subjunguntur ut innocēns (1.5.65); Traupman’s praepositiō per compositiōnem for a prefix (248). Latin prepositions take the accusative or the ablative; Traupman’s formula is praepositiōnēs aut accūsātīvō aut ablātīvō cāsuī serviunt, literally “serve the case” (248), a use of servīre that is not found in Lewis & Short; say rather that a preposition is joined with a case, cum accūsātīvō jungitur.

phrases.latin: ut ad, cum esset praepositiō, d litteram, cum autem conjūnctiō, t acciperet
phrases.english: that ad should take a d when it was a preposition, and a t when it was a conjunction

phrases.latin: compositae aut praepositiōnibus subjunguntur ut innocēns
phrases.english: compound words either have prefixes put before them, like innocēns
The preposition “ad” takes the accusative case.

phrases.latin: Praepositiōnēs aut accūsātīvō aut ablātīvō cāsuī serviunt.
phrases.english: Prepositions take either the accusative or the ablative case.
